paper.title: Parental Assortative Mating and the Intergenerational Transmission of Human Capital
paper.journal: Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Dipartimento di Economia e Finanza, Working Paper Series n. 101 (ISSN 2704-7407)
paper.code_data_availability: Not stated. The paper reports only that it uses administrative registers of the Danish population (the civil register linked to the education register, data sourced in early 2018) and acknowledges funding from the Danish Council for …

registers.name_in_paper: the civil register (the Danish civil registration system, established 1968)
registers.years: 1968 onwards (parent-child linkage complete for children born 1956 or later)
registers.role: linkage and sample frame: the unique personal identification number links all national registers and identifies family quartets of two parents and their first two children

registers.name_in_paper: the education register (Danish education registers; qualifications reported by educational institutions to the Ministry of Education)
registers.years: qualifications obtained before 1971 are self-reports from the 1970 population census; from 1971 institutions report to the Ministry of Education; data sourced in early 2018
registers.role: the single measured variable: educational attainment (years of education) of every family member, which is both the treatment and the outcome of every claim
variables_mentioned: normed duration of a qualification by the shortest route

linkages: all national registers are linked by the unique personal identification number issued under the civil registration system
family quartets (father, mother, first child, second child) formed from the parent-child links in the civil register
the civil register is matched with the education register to obtain educational attainment for every member of the quartet

sample.universe: the full population of Danish families with at least two children and parents born from 1920 (the first birth year for which educational information exists) to 1979
sample.unit_of_observation: family quartet (father, mother, first child, second child); in the Table 3 OLS regressions the unit is the child, with both children of each family included
selection_rules: full population of Danish families with at least two children, parents born 1920-1979: 639,516 families
exclude families for which either parent was younger than 18 at the birth of a child: 624,883 families

select families where a child is born in 1956 or later (the first year the parent-child linkage is complete) and the second child is born in 1988 or earlier (the last birth year for which attainment at age 29 is observed, data having been sourced in early 2018): 530,390 families
drop families with sibling age spacing smaller than one year or larger than ten years (the first and last percentile of the spacing distribution): 524,577 families
drop families whose first child was born after 1978, to allow a maximum sibling spacing of ten years also among younger families: 477,953 families
exclude families with either parent born after 1951, to avoid selectivity into early parenthood among later cohorts: 432,715 families
drop families with missing information on educational attainment for any member: estimating sample of 417,746 families and 1,670,984 individuals
sample.period: parents born 1920-1951 and their first two children born 1956-1988; educational attainment measured at age 29; data sourced in early 2018
sample.n_observations: 1,670,984 individuals in 417,746 family quartets; 1,297 empirical correlation moments in the minimum-distance estimation; 835,492 child observations in the Table 3 OLS regressions

construction_notes: Educational attainment is imputed from the qualification with the highest normed duration on October 31 in the year of turning 29, using Ministry of Education norms for the time to obtain each qualification by the shortest route.

Educational qualifications obtained before 1971 are self-reports from the 1970 population census; from 1971 educational institutions report qualifications to the Ministry of Education (Jensen and Rasmussen, 2011).
Years of education are residualized on year-of-birth dummies throughout the analysis to remove common trends that could induce spurious patterns of correlation.

Individuals are grouped into non-overlapping three-year birth cohorts, each indicated by its central year; mean attainment grew by about 4.5 years and its standard deviation fell by about 1 year over the 66 years spanned by the first and last cohort.

Empirical correlations are computed by family type (mixed-gender, all sons, all daughters) and by combination of birth cohorts of the two family members, after excluding cells with fewer than 100 pairs; bootstrapped standard errors of these correlations weight the minimum-distance problem.

In the Table 3 OLS regressions all variables are measured as deviations from generational means, so no constant is included, both children of each family enter, and standard errors are clustered at the family level.
Robustness checks mentioned but not reported (footnote 2): extending the sample to half siblings, and using the second and third rather than the first and second children.

claims.statement: An additional year of father's education is associated with 0.201 more years of child education in an OLS regression that does not condition on the mother's education.

register_source.value: the education register linked to the civil register on the personal identification number (UDDA / Danish education registers, Jensen and Rasmussen 2011); no DST variable name is given in the paper

estimand.target_population: children in the Danish family quartets of the estimating sample; the authors present these as benchmark associations and state that the single-parent coefficients confound the parent's direct effect with parental assortative mating

population.period: parents born 1920-1951 and their first two children born 1956-1988; educational attainment observed at age 29, data sourced in early 2018
population.selection: families with at least two children and both parents observed; either parent younger than 18 at the birth of a child excluded; a child born 1956 or later and the second child born 1988 or earlier; sibling age spacing between one and ten years; first child born by 1978; either parent born after 1951 excluded; families with missing education for any member dropped

identification.source_of_variation: none: a cross-sectional OLS association between the education of family members in the population of Danish family quartets

key_assumptions.assumption: The OLS coefficient from regressing child education on one parent's education in isolation from the spouse is a convolution of the direct effect of that parent and the impact of parental assortative mating: no causal interpretation of the coefficient is claimed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors attribute the point to Holmlund, Lindahl and Plug (2011) and offer the contrast with Column (3), where including both parents lowers each coefficient by about a third, as evidence that assortative mating is at work.

key_assumptions.assumption: All variables are measured as deviations from generational means, so the regressions include no constant and the coefficients are comparable across generations.
Residualizing years of education on year-of-birth dummies removes the common trends in education that would otherwise induce spurious patterns of correlation between family members.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Supported only by the descriptive evidence of Table 1 that mean attainment grew by about 4.5 years and its standard deviation fell by about 1 year over the 66 years spanned by the cohorts.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimating sample is conditioned on the family structure and birth-year windows set out in Section 2 (at least two children, both parents born 1920-1951, sibling spacing of one to ten years, first child born 1956-1978, second child born by 1988, complete education for all four members), so the estimates describe this conditioned population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors motivate the parental birth-year cut at 1951 by selectivity into early parenthood among later cohorts, and report in footnote 2 that conclusions are robust to alternative sampling schemes (half siblings; second and third rather than first and second children).

threats_discussed: the single-parent coefficient is a convolution of the parent's direct effect and parental assortative mating (Holmlund, Lindahl and Plug 2011)
even with both parents included, the OLS contrast gives no measure of the assortative-mating effect, which is why the paper estimates a structural correlations model instead
robustness_checks: Columns (1)-(4) of Table 3 vary the conditioning set (one parent, both parents, both parents plus their interaction)
the implied intergenerational correlation obtained by rescaling the coefficient with the ratio of parent and child standard deviations is compared with the raw correlation of Table 2
unresolved_confounders: parental assortative mating, which the authors state the OLS coefficients cannot separate from each parent's direct contribution

estimator.value: OLS

estimation.specification: OLS regression of child years of education on parental years of education, both children of each family included; all variables measured as deviations from generational means so the regression includes no constant
fixed_effects: year-of-birth dummies (years of education residualized on them)
estimation.clustering: robust standard errors clustered at the level of the family

source_table.value: Table 3, column (1)

adjustment_set.label: year-of-birth dummies (years of education residualized on them)
generational means (all variables in deviations from them)

evidence.how: Table 3 prints a coefficient and a standard error for every column and nothing else: no confidence interval, confidence level, p-value or significance star is reported.

No baseline mean or standard deviation of the dependent variable is printed for Table 3. The outcome is child years of education residualized on year-of-birth dummies and measured as a deviation from the generational mean; Table 1 reports the mean (12.30) and standard deviation (3.04) of raw years of education pooled over all family roles and birth cohorts, which is not the mean of this outcome.

Looked for a generalisation claim: the authors state where the data come from (Denmark, over 400,000 families) but nowhere claim a domain beyond the estimated population over which the finding is said to hold.
Table 3 prints no stars or p-values. |coefficient| / standard error = 0.201 / 0.001 = 201.00, compared with the conventional 1.96 two-sided 5% critical value.

key_assumptions.assumption: The human-capital generating factors of equations (1) and (2) are zero-mean and mutually orthogonal, so that within-family educational correlations are functions only of the variances of the shared factors and not of the idiosyncratic ones.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered; the orthogonal factor structure is imposed as the definition of the model.

formal.as_written: y_ij = a_ij + γ_Aj + γ_H(i)j + μ_j, H(i) = F, M   (1);  y_ij = a_ij + γ_Aj + γ_Mj + γ_Fj + γ_Mj γ_Fj + θ_j, H(i) = C₁, C₂   (2)

key_assumptions.assumption: Mixed-gender siblings share only factors stemming from the family environment: the intragenerational sibling component θ is zero for mixed-gender sibling pairs. The difference in educational correlations between same-gender and mixed-gender children identifies σ²_θ and, with it, the remaining parameters of the otherwise under-identified system.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors appeal to evidence that interactions independent of the family occur predominantly among same-gender peers (Martin and Fabes 2001; Fabes et al. 2003), and to the lower raw educational correlations of mixed-gender than same-gender siblings in Table 2; they argue the same-gender estimates are an upper bound for mixed-gender pairs.

formal.as_written: θ_j = 0 if g_ij ≠ g_i′j;  H(i) = C₁, H(i′) = C₂   (6)

key_assumptions.assumption: No sorting of families across schools and communities: each of the intergenerationally transmitted factors γ is orthogonal to the intragenerational sibling factor θ.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested here; the authors cite Bingley, Cappellari and Tatsiramos (2021), where sorting is identified from the timing of families' mobility across communities and community effects are found to be overestimated when sorting is ignored, and therefore treat θ as an upper bound.

a saturated interaction of family type with all parameters would re-introduce under-identification, so σ²_μ is restricted to be constant across family types in Panel (B)

No baseline or control-group mean and no standard deviation of the outcome is reported. The outcome is a correlation coefficient between family members; the paper prints no pre-period or control-group counterpart for it, and the summary statistics of Table 1 report only the mean and standard deviation of years of education by birth cohort.

Looked for a generalisation claim: the authors state where the data come from (Denmark, over 400,000 families) but nowhere claim a domain beyond the estimated population over which the finding is said to hold.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested here; the authors cite Bingley, Cappellari and Tatsiramos (2021), where sorting is identified from the timing of families' mobility across communities and community effects are found to be overestimated when sorting is ignored, and therefore treat θ as an upper bound.

key_assumptions.assumption: Residualizing years of education on year-of-birth dummies removes the common trends in education that would otherwise induce spurious patterns of correlation between family members.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Supported only by the descriptive evidence of Table 1 that mean attainment grew by about 4.5 years and its standard deviation fell by about 1 year over the 66 years spanned by the cohorts.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimating sample is conditioned on the family structure and birth-year windows set out in Section 2 (at least two children, both parents born 1920-1951, sibling spacing of one to ten years, first child born 1956-1978, second child born by 1988, complete education for all four members), so the estimates describe this conditioned population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors motivate the parental birth-year cut at 1951 by selectivity into early parenthood among later cohorts, and report in footnote 2 that conclusions are robust to alternative sampling schemes (half siblings; second and third rather than first and second children).

The paper frames this estimate as an upper bound twice over: the no-sorting assumption makes it an upper bound on influences siblings share independently of parents, and the same-gender estimate is argued to be an upper bound for mixed-gender pairs.

evidence.how: Table 4 prints a coefficient and a standard error for every parameter and nothing else: no confidence interval, confidence level, p-value or significance star is reported anywhere in the paper for these estimates.

No baseline or control-group mean and no standard deviation of the outcome is reported. The outcome is a correlation coefficient between family members; the paper prints no pre-period or control-group counterpart for it, and the summary statistics of Table 1 report only the mean and standard deviation of years of education by birth cohort.

Looked for a generalisation claim: the authors state where the data come from (Denmark, over 400,000 families) but nowhere claim a domain beyond the estimated population over which the finding is said to hold.

key_assumptions.assumption: The human-capital generating factors of equations (1) and (2) are zero-mean and mutually orthogonal, so that within-family educational correlations are functions only of the variances of the shared factors and not of the idiosyncratic ones.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered; the orthogonal factor structure is imposed as the definition of the model.

key_assumptions.assumption: Mixed-gender siblings share only factors stemming from the family environment: the intragenerational sibling component θ is zero for mixed-gender sibling pairs. The difference in educational correlations between same-gender and mixed-gender children identifies σ²_θ and, with it, the remaining parameters of the otherwise under-identified system.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors appeal to evidence that interactions independent of the family occur predominantly among same-gender peers (Martin and Fabes 2001; Fabes et al. 2003), and to the lower raw educational correlations of mixed-gender than same-gender siblings in Table 2; they argue the same-gender estimates are an upper bound for mixed-gender pairs.

formal.as_written: θ_j = 0 if g_ij ≠ g_i′j;  H(i) = C₁, H(i′) = C₂   (6)

key_assumptions.assumption: No sorting of families across schools and communities: each of the intergenerationally transmitted factors γ is orthogonal to the intragenerational sibling factor θ.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested here; the authors cite Bingley, Cappellari and Tatsiramos (2021), where sorting is identified from the timing of families' mobility across communities and community effects are found to be overestimated when sorting is ignored, and therefore treat θ as an upper bound.

key_assumptions.assumption: Residualizing years of education on year-of-birth dummies removes the common trends in education that would otherwise induce spurious patterns of correlation between family members.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Supported only by the descriptive evidence of Table 1 that mean attainment grew by about 4.5 years and its standard deviation fell by about 1 year over the 66 years spanned by the cohorts.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimating sample is conditioned on the family structure and birth-year windows set out in Section 2 (at least two children, both parents born 1920-1951, sibling spacing of one to ten years, first child born 1956-1978, second child born by 1988, complete education for all four members), so the estimates describe this conditioned population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors motivate the parental birth-year cut at 1951 by selectivity into early parenthood among later cohorts, and report in footnote 2 that conclusions are robust to alternative sampling schemes (half siblings; second and third rather than first and second children).

key_assumptions.assumption: In the heterogeneity model the intragenerational assortative mating parameter sigma^2_mu is restricted to be constant across family types, because a saturated interaction of family type with every parameter would re-introduce the under-identification problem of Section 3.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test; the restriction is imposed for identification and the authors say so explicitly.

heterogeneity.dimension: gender composition of the two children (MX / BB / GG)
heterogeneity.finding: the father-specific contribution is about twice as large when both children are sons (0.0556, s.e. 0.0090) as when both are daughters (0.0237, s.e. 0.0093), with mixed-gender families in between (0.0370, s.e. 0.0047); the paper states all differences are statistically significant, at the 10 percent level for mixed vs all-daughters or lower.

ambiguities: Table 4 Panel (B) prints the MX / BB / GG subscripts in a font the PDF text layer does not reproduce; the assignment of the three rows of each parameter to family types is taken from the running text of Section 4.2 and cross-checked against the 72 and 78 percent shares the paper reports for all-son and all-daughter families (evidence e8).

evidence.how: Table 4 prints a coefficient and a standard error for every parameter and nothing else: no confidence interval, confidence level, p-value or significance star is reported anywhere in the paper for these estimates.

No baseline or control-group mean and no standard deviation of the outcome is reported. The outcome is a correlation coefficient between family members; the paper prints no pre-period or control-group counterpart for it, and the summary statistics of Table 1 report only the mean and standard deviation of years of education by birth cohort.

Looked for a generalisation claim: the authors state where the data come from (Denmark, over 400,000 families) but nowhere claim a domain beyond the estimated population over which the finding is said to hold.

Table 4 Panel (B) prints the family-type subscripts (MX, BB, GG) in a font the PDF text layer does not carry, so the three rows of each parameter are distinguished by matching them to the text. The rows run MX, BB, GG in order: the text states the mother-specific contribution is about a quarter larger for all daughters (0.0392) than for all sons (0.0316), that the father-specific contribution is about twice as large for all sons (0.0556) as for all daughters (0.0237) with mixed in between (0.0370), and that the residual sibling parameter is 0.057 for daughters and 0.030 for sons. The assignment is confirmed arithmetically: with gammaA = 0.2396 for all sons the joint share is 0.2396/0.3286 = 72.9 percent and with gammaA = 0.2376 for all daughters it is 0.2376/0.3015 = 78.8 percent, matching the stated 72 and 78 percent.
The paper prints no stars, p-values or confidence intervals for Table 4. |coefficient| / standard error = 0.0237 / 0.0093 = 2.55, compared with the conventional 1.96 two-sided 5% critical value.

evidence.how: Table 4 prints a coefficient and a standard error for every parameter and nothing else: no confidence interval, confidence level, p-value or significance star is reported anywhere in the paper for these estimates.

No baseline or control-group mean and no standard deviation of the outcome is reported. The outcome is a correlation coefficient between family members; the paper prints no pre-period or control-group counterpart for it, and the summary statistics of Table 1 report only the mean and standard deviation of years of education by birth cohort.

Looked for a generalisation claim: the authors state where the data come from (Denmark, over 400,000 families) but nowhere claim a domain beyond the estimated population over which the finding is said to hold.

Table 4 Panel (B) prints the family-type subscripts (MX, BB, GG) in a font the PDF text layer does not carry, so the three rows of each parameter are distinguished by matching them to the text. The rows run MX, BB, GG in order: the text states the mother-specific contribution is about a quarter larger for all daughters (0.0392) than for all sons (0.0316), that the father-specific contribution is about twice as large for all sons (0.0556) as for all daughters (0.0237) with mixed in between (0.0370), and that the residual sibling parameter is 0.057 for daughters and 0.030 for sons. The assignment is confirmed arithmetically: with gammaA = 0.2396 for all sons the joint share is 0.2396/0.3286 = 72.9 percent and with gammaA = 0.2376 for all daughters it is 0.2376/0.3015 = 78.8 percent, matching the stated 72 and 78 percent.
The paper prints no stars, p-values or confidence intervals for Table 4. |coefficient| / standard error = 0.0575 / 0.0122 = 4.71, compared with the conventional 1.96 two-sided 5% critical value.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested here; the authors cite Bingley, Cappellari and Tatsiramos (2021), where sorting is identified from the timing of families' mobility across communities and community effects are found to be overestimated when sorting is ignored, and therefore treat θ as an upper bound.

key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors motivate the parental birth-year cut at 1951 by selectivity into early parenthood among later cohorts, and report in footnote 2 that conclusions are robust to alternative sampling schemes (half siblings; second and third rather than first and second children).

key_assumptions.assumption: Each component of the educational correlations evolves linearly in birth cohort; parental parameters are trended on the cohort of the elder parent and child correlations on the cohort of the elder sibling.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue from the raw cohort profiles of Figure 1 that simple linear trends should not be overly restrictive; no formal test of linearity is reported.

No baseline or control-group mean and no standard deviation of the outcome is reported. The outcome is a correlation coefficient between family members; the paper prints no pre-period or control-group counterpart for it, and the summary statistics of Table 1 report only the mean and standard deviation of years of education by birth cohort.

Looked for a generalisation claim: the authors state where the data come from (Denmark, over 400,000 families) but nowhere claim a domain beyond the estimated population over which the finding is said to hold.

evidence.annotation: Note: The graph plots predicted correlation coefficients of years of education between parents and children and their decomposition into the factors that are transmitted jointly by both parents and the factors that are transmitted individually by each parent. The shaded areas are the 95% confidence intervals of the predictions. The line labelled InterG shows the total intergenerational correlation resulting from the sum of all the factors that are passed from parents to children; the line labelled PAM InterG shows the factors that are transmitted jointly by the parents; the line labelled Father InterG shows the factors that are transmitted only by the father; the line labelled Mother InterG shows the factors that are transmitted only by the mother. The line labelled Complementarity shows the product of the father and mother-specific factors. Correlations are estimated from the model with cohort trends of Section 4.3.

evidence.how: The paper prints no stars, p-values or confidence intervals for Table 4. |coefficient| / standard error = 0.0007 / 0.0003 = 2.33, compared with the conventional 1.96 two-sided 5% critical value.

key_assumptions.assumption: The human-capital generating factors of equations (1) and (2) are zero-mean and mutually orthogonal, so that within-family educational correlations are functions only of the variances of the shared factors and not of the idiosyncratic ones.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test is offered; the orthogonal factor structure is imposed as the definition of the model.

key_assumptions.assumption: Mixed-gender siblings share only factors stemming from the family environment: the intragenerational sibling component θ is zero for mixed-gender sibling pairs. The difference in educational correlations between same-gender and mixed-gender children identifies σ²_θ and, with it, the remaining parameters of the otherwise under-identified system.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors appeal to evidence that interactions independent of the family occur predominantly among same-gender peers (Martin and Fabes 2001; Fabes et al. 2003), and to the lower raw educational correlations of mixed-gender than same-gender siblings in Table 2; they argue the same-gender estimates are an upper bound for mixed-gender pairs.

formal.as_written: θ_j = 0 if g_ij ≠ g_i′j;  H(i) = C₁, H(i′) = C₂   (6)

key_assumptions.assumption: No sorting of families across schools and communities: each of the intergenerationally transmitted factors γ is orthogonal to the intragenerational sibling factor θ.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not tested here; the authors cite Bingley, Cappellari and Tatsiramos (2021), where sorting is identified from the timing of families' mobility across communities and community effects are found to be overestimated when sorting is ignored, and therefore treat θ as an upper bound.

key_assumptions.assumption: Residualizing years of education on year-of-birth dummies removes the common trends in education that would otherwise induce spurious patterns of correlation between family members.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Supported only by the descriptive evidence of Table 1 that mean attainment grew by about 4.5 years and its standard deviation fell by about 1 year over the 66 years spanned by the cohorts.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimating sample is conditioned on the family structure and birth-year windows set out in Section 2 (at least two children, both parents born 1920-1951, sibling spacing of one to ten years, first child born 1956-1978, second child born by 1988, complete education for all four members), so the estimates describe this conditioned population.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors motivate the parental birth-year cut at 1951 by selectivity into early parenthood among later cohorts, and report in footnote 2 that conclusions are robust to alternative sampling schemes (half siblings; second and third rather than first and second children).

key_assumptions.assumption: Each component of the educational correlations evolves linearly in birth cohort; parental parameters are trended on the cohort of the elder parent and child correlations on the cohort of the elder sibling.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue from the raw cohort profiles of Figure 1 that simple linear trends should not be overly restrictive; no formal test of linearity is reported.

evidence.annotation: Note: The graph plots predicted correlation coefficients of years of education between parents and children and their decomposition into the factors that are transmitted jointly by both parents and the factors that are transmitted individually by each parent. The shaded areas are the 95% confidence intervals of the predictions. The line labelled InterG shows the total intergenerational correlation resulting from the sum of all the factors that are passed from parents to children; the line labelled PAM InterG shows the factors that are transmitted jointly by the parents; the line labelled Father InterG shows the factors that are transmitted only by the father; the line labelled Mother InterG shows the factors that are transmitted only by the mother. The line labelled Complementarity shows the product of the father and mother-specific factors. Correlations are estimated from the model with cohort trends of Section 4.3.
